    Key Points

    Digital lives: why we protect data and systems

    • Digital networks bring speed and convenience, and they also spread our information across more organisations than before.
    • Look at impact on three levels: individuals, groups and organisations.
    • We protect data and systems to keep three promises: confidentiality, integrity and availability.
    • Attackers often target the person using a system, because it is easier than breaking the technology.
    • The harm from an attack spreads, so separate the people hurt first from the people hurt later.

    Social engineering: hacking the human

    • Social engineering attacks trust, habits and emotions instead of technology.
    • Attackers pull levers such as authority, urgency, fear, helpfulness, curiosity and reward, often in combination. Feeling rushed is a warning sign.
    • Name a tactic by what the attacker does: a fake message is phishing, an invented story is pretexting, a tempting object is baiting, following through a door is tailgating, and a trade of favours is quid pro quo.
    • Attacks follow four stages: research, building trust, the exploit and the exit.
    • Slow down, check by a different route, and report quickly. A fast report is a good outcome.

    Identity, identity management and identity theft

    • An online identity has three parts: attributes (who you are), credentials (how you prove it) and accounts (where you use it). Attributes cannot be replaced, and credentials can.
    • Identity theft means using someone’s details to pretend to be them. The harm spreads from the individual to their group and to the organisations that were fooled.
    • Authentication checks who you are, and authorisation decides what you may open. Multi-factor means two or more different kinds of proof.
    • Least privilege means each person gets the access their job needs and no more.
    • Access should follow the job through joiner, mover and leaver steps, and each step needs an owner.

    The insider threat

    • An insider is anyone with legitimate access, including contractors, volunteers and former staff whose access was never closed.
    • There are three types: malicious (on purpose), negligent (by accident) and compromised (a victim whose access is used by an outsider).
    • To sort a case, ask whether the person meant to cause harm and knew it was happening.
    • You cannot remove the insider threat, but you can reduce, detect and respond, with controls that fit the type: least privilege, prompt account closing, multi-factor authentication, two-person approval, logging, and making the safe way easy.
    • Espionage is spying for a business or a government. It usually involves crime, and it uses the same human tactics as social engineering. If you are approached, say no and tell your manager or security team.

    Attack techniques and human defences

    • Direct access means reaching a device, room or paper in person: tailgating, shoulder surfing, walk-up access, baiting and bin raiding. The best defences are habits: challenge, lock, never plug in, shred.
    • Phishing and pretexting use urgency, authority and trust. The human defence is pause, verify through a channel you already trust, and report with no blame.
    • Identity theft is an outcome. Account takeover with a reused password is one technique that can lead to it.
    • No single defence is enough. Technology and people work as layers, and people are often the last layer.
    • Espionage, bribed insiders and phishing all use human weaknesses, so the same human defences apply.

    Privacy and privacy impact assessments

    • Information privacy means knowing what is collected about you, how it is used and who it is shared with, and having a say.
    • When privacy fails, harms follow: lost money, stolen identity, embarrassment or unfair treatment, risk of being found, and lost trust. They spread from individuals to groups and organisations.
    • Organisations carry most of the duty for privacy, but individuals carry some: share only what a service needs, and care for other people’s information.
    • A good response is both ethical (who is affected, what is fair) and practical (who does what, by when, and how it is checked).
    • A threshold assessment is a quick, written check that decides whether a project needs a full PIA. Sensitivity, children, new technology and outside companies all point towards a full PIA.

    Social media and what attackers can build from it

    • One post is a piece. A whole profile is the picture, and an attacker can join facts, patterns, relationships, feelings and answers to build a believable story.
    • Other people’s posts about you count too, so check before you post about them.
    • Cut down what a profile gives away: choose the audience, share only what is needed, use two-step verification, and think about who could use a post.
    • Check a suspect account’s age, name and follower count. If a friend’s account acts oddly, check with them another way, not in the same chat.
    • If you are attacked online: do not argue, save evidence, report, tell someone, and warn others if you are being impersonated.

    People at work: BYOD and working from home

    • People are part of the defence. Technical controls on their own are not enough, and managers who notice, listen and treat people fairly lower the risk more than any filter.
    • Specific, explained social media guidance works better than “never post about work”. Say what not to share and who to ask, and make it safe to admit a mistake.
    • An employer’s control passes the test if it is proportionate to the risk, open to the staff it affects, and about work.
    • Ask two questions of every rule: how much security does it add, and how much burden does it put on people? Rules that are too heavy get worked around.
    • BYOD and working from home need clear rules: updated devices, a separate work app or profile, secure remote access, quick reporting, and removing work data when someone leaves.

    Security awareness that changes behaviour

    • Awareness is what people do on a busy day, not a policy in a folder.
    • Awareness works when it is short, specific, role-based, repeated and safe to report.
    • Check behaviour, such as reports and spot checks, and not attendance. More reports can be a good sign.
    • Your own habits come to work with you, so check your own ICT life privately and choose one small, specific change with a when.
    • Awareness, vetting and access each have a limit, so a good plan uses all three.

    Vetting, trust and access

    • Vetting checks a person before you give them trust and access. It lowers risk, and it is valuable.
    • A check is a snapshot. It finds only what was recorded, and it cannot read intentions, so vetting is one layer and not the whole answer.
    • Ongoing assessment keeps trust under review after hiring, and it works only when staff are treated fairly and privately.
    • Compartmentalisation limits access, knowledge and systems to what each job needs, so one mistake or one bad decision does limited harm.
    • Limits have costs for staff, so plan cover and emergency access, review who has access, explain why, and give every control an owner.

    Australian privacy law and data breaches

    • The Privacy Act and its 13 APPs bind most Australian Government agencies and some private organisations. Many small businesses are outside it, but a private health service provider that holds health information is covered whatever its size.
    • A council-run body is generally covered by state or territory privacy law instead. Find out which law applies before you say what an organisation must do.
    • To pick the APP, ask what stage of the information’s life the problem happened at. Outsiders getting in is usually APP 11. The organisation choosing a new use is usually APP 6, or APP 7 for marketing.
    • For a suspected breach: assess quickly, act to reduce harm, and tell the people affected and the OAIC if serious harm is likely.
    • The 2024 changes added a right to sue for serious invasions of privacy, stronger enforcement and APP 11 wording on technical and organisational measures. The Cyber Security Act 2024 requires some businesses to report ransomware payments within 72 hours.

    Responding to identity theft, and what comes next

    • In identity theft, stop the money first, secure your accounts, get support, check your credit, make a report, replace documents and keep checking.
    • A complaint comes after the urgent steps. Complain to the organisation first, then to the regulator that covers it, and only if the organisation’s handling was part of the problem.
    • Use the number on your card, the official app or a website you type in yourself, never a number or link from a message or caller.
    • Cybercrime lands on people, and experts disagree about where cyber war begins, so define your terms before you argue.
    • Connected devices, big data and quantum computing each change risk in a different way: another device to update, patterns you never chose to share, and a future threat to some encryption.
